outcome: Matthew J. Colbrook (University of Cambridge) posted a preprint, 'Aperiodic maximisers of Lyapunov dimension: a counterexample to the unrestricted form of Eden's conjecture' (Zenodo, 21 September 2026), constructing a polynomial ODE on R^5 with a compact global attractor whose maximal Lyapunov dimension (4+4/c) is attained on an invariant two-torus carrying an irrational (aperiodic) linear flow, strictly exceeding the maximum (3) attained over equilibria and periodic orbits -- directly contradicting the unrestricted statement of Eden's conjecture as given in the Wikipedia bullet. The same maximizing set holds for the finite-time local dimension at every positive time and for the asymptotic Kaplan-Yorke dimension. The result is accompanied by a complete, from-scratch Lean 4 formalization (219 results in Solution.lean plus a 777-theorem supporting 'Eden' library) in a public GitHub repository, restricted to a small trusted axiom set (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) and checked by an independent 'Comparator' tool plus a third-party 'Palomar' verification pipeline.

counterexample.object: A polynomial vector field on R^5 with uniformly negative divergence and a compact global attractor, whose Lyapunov-dimension maximizer is an invariant two-torus carrying an irrational (hence aperiodic) linear flow, rather than any stationary point or periodic orbit.
counterexample.verified_how: Exact singular-value/exact-identity analytic argument in the paper, plus an independent, from-scratch Lean 4 formal verification (219 main results, 777 supporting library theorems) restricted to a small trusted axiom set and cross-checked by an automated Comparator tool and a separate 'Palomar' independent verification pipeline.

summary: The triage record (verdict 'none', checked 2026-09-20) missed this because the result was posted the day after its check (21 September 2026) -- a one-day gap that happens to fall right at the edge of triage timing rather than any error in its searches. I disagree with the triage verdict and set triage_disagreement, though the miss is purely a timing artifact, not a bad search. Colbrook's paper constructs an explicit polynomial ODE on R^5 whose global attractor's maximal Lyapunov dimension is achieved on an aperiodic invariant torus rather than on a stationary point or unstable periodic orbit, which is exactly and precisely a counterexample to the bullet as worded ('the supremum ... is achieved on a stationary point or an unstable periodic orbit'). This is squarely in scope under Sec 3.1: it directly negates the stated claim, not a variant or restricted case. I classify status as 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' because, as of today (22 September 2026), the paper is a one-day-old single-author preprint on Zenodo (not yet on arXiv at the time of my search, and not published in a journal); I found no expert digestion, commentary, blog discussion (Tao's blog, Quanta, Xena Project, etc. all silent on it), or third-party citation discussing or confirming the result. The accompanying from-scratch Lean formalization is extensive and methodologically serious (restricted axiom set, an independent Comparator/Palomar cross-check), which is strong self-verification evidence, but per Sec 6.1 a machine-checked certificate that no outside expert has yet reviewed is 'claimed', not 'resolved' -- soundness bugs in kernels remain possible in principle, and more importantly no human mathematician outside the author is on record as having reviewed the argument. On AI involvement: I found zero evidence, in the Zenodo record, the GitHub repository (README, READING_GUIDE, file listing), or general search, that any AI/ML system (language model, autoformalization tool, Copilot, etc.) was used in constructing either the mathematical argument or the Lean formalization; all methodology descriptions reference only classical tools (Lean/Mathlib, exact analytic identities). I also checked Colbrook's closely related contemporaneous 'computer-assisted counterexample' papers (to the planar Berenstein and Pompeiu-Schiffer conjectures, posted around the same time) to see whether 'computer-assisted' in his usual practice means AI; in the Berenstein paper it explicitly means interval arithmetic and Newton-Kantorovich certification, i.e. not AI, which supports (but does not prove, since it's a different paper) that this is also not AI-involved. Because I could not quote any author statement invoking an AI system, ai_role is 'none' per Sec 6.2's requirement that assisted/generated need the authors' own account.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'resolved' rather than 'claimed' given how thorough and independently cross-checked (Comparator, Palomar) the Lean formalization is -- arguably approaching the bar of a 'published verification by named experts' if the Palomar pipeline constitutes independent third-party review rather than the same author's own additional tooling. I could not determine from available sources whether 'Palomar' is an independent third party or another tool built by Colbrook himself; if it is a genuinely independent verifier, this would push toward 'resolved'. I read the available evidence as the latter (self-built verification infrastructure) given it lives in the same repository under the same authorship with no distinct credited reviewers, but flag the ambiguity.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation of whether 'Palomar' verification is run by an independent party or by Colbrook himself; an arXiv posting or journal submission; any expert commentary, citation, or independent confirmation of the Lean proof (e.g., a second party running the Lean check, or discussion on a mathematical blog/forum); clarification of whether any AI coding assistant was used anywhere in the (extensive, 777+219 theorem) Lean development, which none of the available documentation discloses either way.
